name: mushroomed lentils italian
instructions:
The ITALIAN member of the mushroomed-lentils family — and the rule-breaker: the mushrooms are FINELY DICED, not pureed or processed (chunky, not a goo), and the dish is LIGHTER AND BROTHIER than its siblings.

=== THE BUILD ===

- MUSHROOMS: finely diced — NOT pureed, NOT food-processed. Chunky, not a goo.
- CELERY, CARROT, AND ONION: also finely diced (soffrito).
- LENTILS: whole.
- TOMATO PASTE: the backbone — TOMATO-FORWARD, NO DARK STOCK (walked back; see notes — the stock dominates as leftovers).
- A TOMATO (chunked) is TOLERATED — unlike the more northern siblings, which want no tomato chunk at all.
- POTATO: diced potato is ALLOWED but not required.
- BAY LEAF + SEASONINGS: this version wants BAY LEAF and relies on FENNEL (seed and/or powder) and OLD BAY — and probably NO other herb (see the herb rule).
- NOT HERE: no cream/mustard/ale, no cumin/caraway (those belong to the french and german siblings).
- NOT HERE (vs minestrone): no parmesan element, no green beans, no earthy mixed greens.
notes:
=== THE RULE-BREAKER OF THE FAMILY ===

This version half-follows the mushroomed-lentils patterns — the backbone conforms (tomato paste, though the stock has since left), the texture rebels:
- MUSHROOMS DICED, NOT PUREED: the family's signature move (pureed mushrooms as the gravy engine) is deliberately absent. Here the mushrooms are finely diced and stay CHUNKY — a component, not a goo.
- LIGHTER AND BROTHIER: the big difference vs [[mushroomed-lentils-french]] — the french version relies on the pureed mushrooms + cream/mustard as a FLAVOR ENGINE; this one is a lighter, brothier dish.

=== DARK STOCK — OUT (THE LEFTOVERS TEST) ===

Walked back: the DARK VEGETABLE STOCK IS OUT — this dish is JUST TOMATO-FORWARD now (tomato paste backbone). It tastes good the day you make it with the stock, but AS LEFTOVERS THE STOCK DOMINATES — the rest of the dish is so mediterranean/simple that the stock takes over once the flavors merge overnight. (Same florals-fail-cold logic as the german stew's coriander lesson: judge a stew by its leftover state, not its day-one state.) The tomato paste still separates it from the minestrone family, which doesn't like paste as much.

THE TOMATO-CHUNK TOLERANCE: where this version does break from the family — it can TOLERATE A TOMATO in it (chunked), unlike the more northern versions (french/german/british), which want no tomato chunk at all.

FRESH TOMATOES, NOT CANNED: the tomato has to be FRESH for this to work. Canned doesn't work as good — it's TOO SAUCY. (Same rule as [[minestrone-soup]].) A BOX OF CHERRY TOMATOES is usually perfect — they're lighter.

=== FAT — BUTTER VS OLIVE OIL, UNDECIDED HERE ===

In all the mushroomed lentils, BUTTER > OLIVE OIL — but for this one I'm not certain (the lighter/brothier italian register may be the exception). Next cook: A MIX OF BOTH.

=== LEMON JUICE — A LITTLE, NO ZEST ===

This dish likes A LITTLE LEMON JUICE (not zest). [[minestrone-soup]] does NOT — another divider between the two italian legume soups.

=== BAY LEAF IS NON-NEGOTIABLE ===

Forgetting the bay leaf is CATASTROPHIC — in this soup and in [[minestrone-soup]] both.

=== SEASONINGS — FENNEL + OLD BAY ===

This version leans on seasonings where its siblings lean on balancer kits: FENNEL SEED/POWDER and OLD BAY. No cream/mustard (french kit), no ale/pickle (german kit), no cumin/caraway (german seeds).

=== VS MINESTRONE ===

Distinct from [[minestrone-soup]] despite the italian soffrito + legume shape: no parmesan cheese element, no green beans, no earthy mixed greens — and tomato PASTE where minestrone wants whole tomato.

=== THE FAMILY ===

- [[mushroomed-lentils-french]]: pureed mushrooms + cream/mustard flavor engine — the rich pole; this is the light pole.
- [[mushroomed-lentils-german]]: ale + pickle + cumin/caraway.
- [[mushroomed-lentils-british]]: the wellington (A) and the pub stew (B — rosemary/thyme/lemon/potato + ale/marmite).

=== FAMILY HERB RULE (REVISED) — ROSEMARY NEEDS THE DARK ANCHOR ===

Cooked again and revised: within this family, ROSEMARY BELONGS ONLY WHERE ALE/MARMITE LIVE — in the british/german versions it gives LIFT against the darker, more complex anchor. In the french and italian versions rosemary tastes ORTHOGONAL — nothing pairs with it; it's just standing there. (Though the dark-anchor theory is itself specious as a general rule — rosemary works in plenty of dishes without one, chicken dishes in general. Maybe the real requirement is just 'SOMETHING MEATY' for it to grip. OR maybe it's the CELERY: the french/italian versions are very celery + tomato forward, and celery is absent in the british/german. But [[chicken-pot-pie]] has celery AND rosemary happily — so that's not a perfect theory either. Unsolved.) The french version likes THYME for its own reasons (mustard + cream). The italian version — lacking any other flavor engine — wants BAY LEAF + the seasonings and probably NO other herb (maybe parsley or an earthy green, but with the stock in play I'm not so sure).
